did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with the heading “A Song of Ascents” and a direct address to the Lord, who is described as “enthroned in heaven.” The speaker expresses his prayer through the image of lifting his eyes upward.
Did you know? The phrase “I lift my eyes to you” describes not only a physical gaze, but also an appeal of trust, prayer, and a request for help from the Lord.

Did you know? The psalm compares the people’s waiting for the Lord to the way servants look to their master’s hand and a maidservant to her mistress’s hand. The image emphasizes dependence, attentiveness, and waiting for a response or assistance.
Did you know? In this verse, the word “our eyes” appears in the plural, showing that the appeal to the Lord is presented as the prayer of a community, not just of one individual.
Did you know? The words “until he shows us mercy” indicate a continued wait for grace. The people do not merely ask; they also persist in waiting for the Lord’s response.
Did you know? The request “Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us” is repeated twice in succession. The repetition intensifies the sense of urgency and the strength of the plea.

Did you know? The reason for the request for mercy is “for we have had more than enough of contempt.” The people describe a situation in which contempt has become so great and prolonged that it fills their experience.

Did you know? At the conclusion, contempt is described with two expressions: “the mockery of the complacent” and “the contempt of the proud.” In this way, the psalm sets the suffering people against the complacent and proud, who treat them with mockery and humiliation.

Did you know? The word “our souls” in the final verse emphasizes that the humiliation is not presented merely as an external event, but as a burden the people feel within themselves and suffer over time.
